recipes.contentMarkdown:
# Mushroom Risotto for Two in 40 Minutes

Two bowls of restaurant-grade risotto in forty minutes — and no, you won't spend the evening chained to the stove.

That promise sounds glib until you've watched a small batch fail for reasons a big batch never does. I learned this the embarrassing way: halve a six-serving risotto, keep its instructions, and your two portions go gluey before the broth even runs out. A small pan of rice sits over the same flame as a large one but holds a fraction of the liquid, so the whole rice-to-heat ratio shifts underneath you. The fix isn't more stirring — it's smaller ladles, a wider pan, and a two-mushroom broth that does most of the flavor work for you. (Dried porcini steeped straight into the stock: ninety seconds of effort that tastes like an afternoon of simmering.)

The Italians have a word for the finished texture — *all'onda*, "like a wave" — and that's the target: spoon the risotto onto a plate, tilt it, and it should ripple back slowly, like the tide going out. Everything in this version is built to get you there on a weeknight, with one saucepan and one wide skillet to wash.

Risotto forgives almost everything except hurry.

## Why This Works: The Starch Science

Risotto's creaminess is chemistry, not cream. Arborio is milled so its outer layers are scuffed while its center stays chalky and dense, and Harold McGee explains in *On Food and Cooking* why that structure is exactly what you want: gentle heat plus steady abrasion coaxes starch out of each grain — amylose to thicken the surrounding liquid, amylopectin for that glossy cling — until the pan becomes its own sauce. No cream, ever.

Three details make or break it. Toasting: America's Test Kitchen found that a minute or two of toasting sets the grain's outer layer so the rice releases starch slowly instead of dissolving into porridge. Broth temperature: Cook's Illustrated tested cold versus hot stock and found cold additions stall the cooking unevenly — I hold mine at a bare simmer, about 180°F (82°C), for the entire cook. And the finish: the Italian *mantecatura*, beating cold butter and finely grated Parmesan into the rice off the heat, creates a true emulsion. Rice gives structure, starch gives body, butter and cheese give the shine.

## Ingredients (and What You Can Swap)

The list is short, which is why each item earns its place. **Arborio rice** — ¾ cup (150 g) for two generous mains — must be a short, round grain with a chalky center; carnaroli works identically and forgives more (see the FAQ). **Two mushrooms, two jobs:** cremini seared hard for browned, meaty edges, plus a small handful of dried porcini dissolved into the broth for the woodsy backbone fresh mushrooms can't manage alone. (A Beautiful Plate's porcini risotto convinced me of this years ago — steeping them in the stock is the whole trick.)

**Wine** deglazes the pan and its acidity keeps the starch in check; no wine on hand? Use broth plus a teaspoon of lemon juice. **Low-sodium vegetable broth** keeps this vegetarian from end to end; chicken broth works if that's not a concern for your table, but use one broth everywhere or the other — mixing muddies the flavor. **Parmesan** should be finely grated on a Microplane so it melts instead of stringing; Grana Padano is the honest stand-in. **Butter is divided** on purpose, and the final tablespoon must go in cold, off the heat, or the emulsion won't set. And never rinse the rice — that starch is the recipe.

## Instructions

One wide 3-quart sauté pan, one small saucepan, forty minutes. Set everything out first — risotto rewards preparation, not improvisation.

### Step 1: Steep the Porcini and Warm the Broth
Pour 4 cups (960 ml) of broth into a small saucepan, add the dried porcini, and bring it to a bare simmer — bubbles hovering at the edges, about 180°F (82°C) — then hold it there. After 10 minutes, lift out the porcini, chop them fine, and set them aside; leave the broth on the lowest flame.

*Chef Augustin's Tip: Park a mug of water next to the stove. Small batches run short on broth sometimes, and hot water tops up the liquid without stalling the rice the way cold tap water would.*

### Step 2: Sear the Mushrooms Until Deeply Golden
Heat 1 tablespoon of the butter with the olive oil in the wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced cremini in a single layer and leave them alone for 3 to 4 minutes — no stirring — until the undersides are deep golden brown. Stir once, cook 2 to 3 minutes more, season with a pinch of salt, and transfer to a plate. Gray, steamed mushrooms mean the pan was crowded or the heat was shy.

### Step 3: Sweat the Onion, Then the Garlic
Drop the heat to medium, melt another tablespoon of butter in the same pan, and scrape the mushroom fond loose from the bottom. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook until translucent, 3 to 4 minutes, then add the garlic for 30 to 60 seconds, just until fragrant. Burnt garlic turns bitter, and there's no coming back.

### Step 4: Toast the Rice
Add the arborio and stir it through the fat for 1 to 2 minutes, until the edges of the grains turn glassy while the centers stay chalk-white and the pan smells faintly nutty, like popcorn about to pop. That glassy edge is your signal: the outer layer is set and the starch will release slowly instead of all at once.

### Step 5: Deglaze With Wine
Pour in the ½ cup (120 ml) of wine and stir until the pan is nearly dry and the raw alcohol smell has cooked off, 1 to 2 minutes. The sizzle lifts the last of the fond off the pan and deposits it straight into the rice.

### Step 6: Build the Risotto, ¼ Cup at a Time
Here's where risotto for two stops following the standard script. Add the simmering broth ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, stirring every 30 seconds or so, and wait until each addition is nearly absorbed — a spoon dragged through should leave a brief dry wake — before adding the next. Full-cup ladles flood a small pan and cook the rice unevenly; quarter-cup ladles keep every grain in the same conversation. Start tasting at 14 minutes. You want al dente: tender, with a barely firm center. You may not need all 4 cups, and that's fine.

*Chef Augustin's Tip: Kenji López-Alt's side-by-side tests on Serious Eats found rice stirred every minute or so absorbs broth just as evenly as rice stirred constantly. Relentless stirring mostly shreds the grains — and your arm.*

### Step 7: Fold Back the Mushrooms
With the final ladle of broth, return the seared cremini along with the chopped porcini and fold them through. Their browned bits re-loosen into the sauce in under a minute.

### Step 8: Mantecatura — the Off-Heat Finish
Pull the pan off the heat entirely. Add the last tablespoon of butter, cold from the fridge, and the ½ cup (50 g) of finely grated Parmesan; stir vigorously for about 30 seconds until the sauce turns glossy and the risotto ripples in a slow wave when you tilt the pan. That wave is *all'onda*. Rest 2 minutes while you warm two bowls.

### Step 9: Adjust and Serve
Risotto waits for no one — it tightens as it sits. Taste, season with salt and black pepper, and loosen with a splash of hot broth if it has moved past wave toward mound. Scatter the thyme over, divide between the warm bowls, and eat immediately, with extra Parmesan within reaching distance.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

Most risotto recipes I've cooked are written for six servings, and the instructions quietly assume that scale. Cut them in half and three things break. The liquid: a recipe calling for 1-cup ladles and 5 to 6 cups of broth expects a big pan with real thermal mass — at ¾ cup of rice, those ladles drown the rice and you stir porridge. The stirring: "stir constantly" is actively harmful at small scale, because the grains grind against each other and burst — that's the glue. The clock: full-size batches run 20 to 25 minutes, but a two-serving batch finishes between 16 and 18, and every minute past al dente is a minute toward baby food. One mistake isn't about rice at all: mushrooms added raw to the pan steam gray and flavorless instead of searing brown. Sear them hard, hold them out, fold them back at the end. Halving ingredients is arithmetic. Halving the technique — ladle size, stirring rhythm, clock — is what nobody writes down.

## Chef's Tips and What I've Learned

Risotto doesn't reward attention; it repays it.

**Chef Augustin's Tip: Grate the Parmesan on a Microplane.** Coarse cheese melts slowly and strings; the fine snow melts into the emulsion in seconds, which matters when you're working off the heat.

**Chef Augustin's Tip: Warm your bowls.** Risotto loses its wave in a cold bowl faster than anywhere else. Thirty seconds under hot tap water buys you minutes at the table.

**Chef Augustin's Tip: Taste the broth before it meets the rice.** If it's already robust, season lightly early and finish the seasoning at the end. Parmesan brings plenty of salt, and it's easier to add than to undo.

What I've learned cooking this on repeat: the recipe is mostly technique, so shop small and buy well. One bunch of arugula with lemon, the glass of Pinot Grigio you cooked with, two shallow bowls — that turns dinner into an evening. The night I stopped chasing extra ingredients and started chasing texture was the night this became a regular instead of a project.

## Your Mushroom Risotto Questions, Answered

### Can I make mushroom risotto for two without wine?
Yes. Swap the ½ cup (120 ml) of wine for ½ cup of broth plus 1 teaspoon of lemon juice or white wine vinegar, added at the same point after toasting. The acid matters more than the wine itself — it keeps the starch in check so the finished dish tastes bright instead of flat. Skipping it entirely still works, but expect a rounder, heavier bowl.

### What can I substitute for arborio rice?
Carnaroli is my first swap: 1:1 by volume, holds its bite confidently, and forgives a distracted minute at the stove. Pearl barley works too but needs 10 to 15 extra minutes and a few more ladles of broth; the result is nuttier and chewier. Sushi rice gets you close to creamy in a pinch. Long-grain rice like basmati will not work — those grains stay separate by design, so no stirring coaxes out the starch.

### Is mushroom risotto for two a balanced dinner?
I think of it the way an Italian grandmother would: a modest bowl of rice, mushrooms, broth, and cheese served as a complete main, not a side. One batch here uses ¾ cup (150 g) of rice, 8 oz (225 g) of mushrooms, and about 2 tablespoons of butter split across two servings — dinner proportions, not restaurant mega-bowls. Round out the plate with a bitter-green salad or roasted asparagus, which is how I serve it most weeknights.

### Can you freeze mushroom risotto?
I don't recommend it. Risotto is an emulsion — rice starch suspended in broth, butter, and cheese — and freezing breaks that suspension: the water separates on thawing, the grains split, and you're left with broken rice in a watery puddle. Refrigerate instead (see below). If you do end up with extra, repurpose it: chilled risotto rolled into balls around a cube of mozzarella and fried makes supplì, leftover risotto's best second act.

### How long does mushroom risotto last in the fridge?
Cool it quickly, then store it airtight for 3 to 4 days — the standard window for cooked leftovers, rice included. Reheat low and slow in a pan with a few tablespoons of broth or water, stirring until it's steaming all the way through and loosened back to a flowing consistency. The texture will be denser than night one, since rice keeps drinking liquid in the fridge, but fresh Parmesan and black pepper bring most of it back.

### What should I serve with mushroom risotto for two?
Contrast is the whole plan. A bitter greens salad — arugula or frisée with a sharp lemon vinaigrette — cuts through the richness. For something warm, asparagus roasted at 425°F (218°C) for 10 to 12 minutes with olive oil and lemon keeps the evening easy, and blistered green beans with garlic take 8 minutes in the same skillet while the risotto rests. Pour the same crisp Pinot Grigio you cooked with. Skip the bread; the rice is the starch.

## Two Bowls, No Leftovers

The window over the stove fogs up, the pots go in the sink, and the table holds two warm bowls of something that ripples when tilted. One of you reaches for the Parmesan without asking. This is the [easy date-night dinner](/recipes/easy-dinner-recipes-for-two) I cook most often — no reservation, no clock to beat, just forty minutes and a wooden spoon doing exactly what you ask of them. The wave waits for one thing only: you, at the table.

recipes.metaDescription: This vegetable stir fry for two comes together in 22 minutes with frozen vegetables, a six-ingredient sauce, and one skillet. Big flavor, no soggy vegetables.
recipes.excerpt: One hot skillet, a bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables, and a sauce measured to the tablespoon: true two-serving stir fry that sears instead of steams, in 22 minutes flat.
recipes.contentMarkdown:
# 22-Minute Vegetable Stir Fry for Two

A bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables, one screaming-hot skillet, and a sauce measured to the tablespoon — that is the entire plan.

Most [stir fry](/recipes/easy-to-make-asian-food-recipes) recipes I've cooked from are written for a table of six. When I halve them, two things break: a small batch of cold vegetables in a big pan never gets hot enough to sear, and the sauce — eyeballed rather than measured — turns into soup at the bottom. This recipe is built for two from the first tablespoon. The vegetable quantities, the sauce ratio, and the cooking order are all scaled to a 12-inch skillet and two plates, and it leans on the bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables already in your freezer, which keeps prep to ten minutes. The technique here — sear hard, sauce late — is one you will reuse every single week.

Stir fry is not a recipe so much as a sequence. Learn the order, and you can improvise the rest forever.

## Why This Works

A stir fry lives or dies at the surface of the pan. Vegetables sear when the cooking surface sits above roughly 350°F (175°C); below that, they release moisture faster than the pan can boil it away, and they end up simmering in their own liquid instead of charring at the edges. I've watched the surface of an overcrowded skillet fall from about 500°F (260°C) to under 350°F (175°C) the moment a full family-size batch went in — that is the steam-braise zone, and it is why crowded stir fry tastes wet and gray instead of blistered and sweet.

Frozen stir-fry vegetables solve the prep problem but create a moisture problem. They are blanched before freezing, so their cell walls are already tender; the only obstacle is the film of ice on every piece. That is why this recipe adds them straight from the freezer in a single layer and leaves them alone for two full minutes — the ice evaporates with a hiss, the surfaces dry out, and then they sear. Thaw them first and you are cooking vegetables that are already half soft.

The sauce is where Harold McGee's *On Food and Cooking* earns its shelf space: cornstarch reaches full thickening power just below a simmer, which is why the glaze goes from milky to glossy in the last twenty seconds. Pour it around the hot perimeter of the pan — where the metal is hottest — and it sets on contact instead of pooling in the middle.

I've cooked this exact recipe in nonstick, cast iron, and carbon steel. Carbon steel wins because it recovers its temperature in seconds after the cold vegetables hit; cast iron is a close second; thin nonstick struggles to hold 400°F (200°C).

Heat is an ingredient here. Everything else is negotiable.

## Ingredients

The sauce for two is measured to the tablespoon: three tablespoons soy sauce, one tablespoon rice vinegar, two teaspoons each of toasted sesame oil, sugar, and cornstarch, plus two tablespoons of water. That ratio clings to twelve ounces of vegetables without pooling. Scale a family-size sauce by feel and it overwhelms a small pan — this is the single biggest fix in the recipe.

Substitutions, each with the fix built in: no rice vinegar? Use white wine vinegar or lime juice — start with two teaspoons, since both run sharper, and the balance still lands. No cornstarch? One tablespoon of all-purpose flour thickens the same volume; the glaze will be slightly cloudy and just as good. Tamari swaps in for soy sauce one-for-one if you cook gluten-free, and honey replaces the sugar at one and a half teaspoons.

One oil note: use regular or light olive oil, not extra-virgin. This pan runs around 400°F (200°C), and extra-virgin gives up its composure right in that neighborhood — I have filled my kitchen with acrid smoke testing exactly this. Light olive oil sat quietly through the same test.

- 2 cups (330g) cooked white rice, warm — leftover, or start it before you prep
- 3 tablespoons (45ml) soy sauce — low-sodium works well, since the sauce reduces
- 1 tablespoon (15ml) rice vinegar
- 2 teaspoons (10ml) toasted sesame oil
- 2 teaspoons (8g) cornstarch
- 2 teaspoons (8g) sugar
- 2 tablespoons (30ml) water
- 2 tablespoons (30ml) olive oil (regular or light, not extra-virgin), divided
- 1 small yellow onion (150g), halved and sliced
- 1 red bell pepper (150g), cored and sliced into strips
- 12 oz (340g) frozen stir-fry vegetables, straight from the freezer
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 teaspoon (5g) fresh ginger, grated
- 2 scallions, thinly sliced, for garnish
- 1 teaspoon (3g) toasted sesame seeds, for garnish

Measure the sauce. A stir fry for two has no room for a missing tablespoon.

## Instructions

### Step 1: Whisk the Sauce First
Combine the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, sugar, cornstarch, and water in a small bowl and whisk until no cornstarch lumps remain — the mixture should look like weak coffee with a chalky undertone, which is exactly right. Set it beside the stove; it goes in at the very end.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Cornstarch settles within a minute. Re-whisk the sauce immediately before it hits the pan, or you will pour off watery liquid and leave the thickener stuck to the bowl. I have watched a perfect pan sauce turn lumpy from exactly this shortcut.

### Step 2: Heat the Pan Until It Is Actually Hot
Set a 12-inch cast iron, carbon steel, or heavy stainless skillet over medium-high heat and add one tablespoon of the olive oil. Heat until the oil shimmers and thins out like water, about three minutes. Flick in a drop of water — if it skitters across the surface and vanishes on contact, the pan sits at roughly 400°F (200°C) and is ready.

### Step 3: Sear the Onion and Pepper
Add the onion and bell pepper, spread them into a single layer, and then do nothing for two minutes. Undisturbed vegetables blister and spot with brown; fussed-over vegetables steam. After the pause, stir-fry for two more minutes, until the onion turns translucent at the edges and both vegetables pick up color.

### Step 4: Add the Frozen Vegetables, Straight From the Freezer
Add the frozen stir-fry vegetables in a single layer — no thawing, no rinsing — and leave them undisturbed for two minutes while the surface ice evaporates with a hiss. Then stir-fry for three to four minutes, until everything is hot through, the pan is nearly dry, and the edges of the broccoli and carrots have browned.

Chef Augustin's Tip: If liquid pools in the pan, the surface has dropped below the searing point. Raise the heat and stir less — patience sears, fussing stews.

### Step 5: Bloom the Garlic and Ginger
Push the vegetables up the sides to clear a well in the center, add the remaining tablespoon of olive oil, then the garlic and ginger. Stir constantly for about forty-five seconds, until the pan smells fragrant and the garlic is barely golden. Garlic's sugars scorch within seconds of that moment, so have the sauce standing by.

### Step 6: Sauce and Glaze
Re-whisk the sauce and pour it around the hot perimeter of the pan, not into the center. Toss constantly for one to two minutes as it thickens just below a simmer, turning from milky to glossy, until the glaze clings to every piece and pools only slightly at the edges.

### Step 7: Plate It Hot
Divide the warm rice between two bowls, spoon the stir fry over, and finish with scallions and sesame seeds. Serve immediately — the vegetables hold their snap for minutes, not quarters of an hour.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

The mistake I keep seeing in small-batch stir fry is a sauce written for six and eyeballed for two. A family-size recipe might call for a third of a cup of soy sauce alongside heaps of vegetables; scaled down carelessly, that same generosity drowns a twelve-ounce bag. Measure the sauce — three tablespoons of soy, not a splash — and the pan stays glossy instead of soupy.

Second: thawing or rinsing frozen vegetables before they hit the pan. They are already blanched; water is the one thing they cannot absorb gracefully. Straight from the freezer, hot dry pan, single layer — that is the whole trick.

Third: a pan that is too small. Twelve ounces of vegetables plus an onion and a pepper need a 12-inch skillet to sit in one layer. In an 8-inch pan the same batch stacks three deep, the surface temperature collapses, and everything steams.

Fourth: extra-virgin olive oil in a searing-hot pan, and garlic in from the first second. Aromatics added at the start burn long before dense carrots turn tender — they belong in a clear well, in the last forty-five seconds.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

Chef Augustin's Tip: Trust the water test. When a flicked droplet skitters instead of spreading, the surface is around 400°F (200°C) — hot enough to evaporate vegetable moisture as fast as the vegetables release it. That balance point is the entire difference between searing and stewing.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Get everything within reach before the oil goes in. A stir fry moves in thirty-second windows and the pan only goes forward — there is no pausing to hunt for the sesame oil while garlic sits on hot metal. Sauce whisked, rice warm, garnish chopped, bowls out.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Season at the end, not the beginning. The sauce reduces as it glazes and concentrates its salt; taste after Step 6 and adjust with a few drops of soy sauce or a splash of vinegar before anything reaches the table.

One habit that changed my weeknights: I keep peeled ginger in the freezer and grate it straight into the pan, frozen. It is faster than mincing, it never molds in the crisper drawer, and it blooms in the hot oil in seconds.

A stir fry rewards the cook who is ready, not the cook who is careful.

## Vegetable Stir Fry for Two: Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I use fresh vegetables instead of frozen?
Yes, and fresh sears even more cleanly. For two, aim for about twelve ounces total: one cup broccoli florets, one carrot cut into coins, one cup snap peas or bell pepper strips. Cook in order of density — carrots and broccoli for three to four minutes, then the tender vegetables for two — and keep everything else identical. The sauce stays the same either way; it is calibrated to twelve ounces of vegetables, frozen or fresh.

### Why are my frozen stir-fry vegetables soggy?
Three usual causes. The vegetables were thawed before cooking, which pushes already-blanched cell walls past soft. The pan was not hot enough when they went in, so they simmered in their own meltwater. Or they were stirred constantly, which keeps surfaces wet and never lets them brown. Fix all three at once: screaming-hot pan, straight from the freezer, a single layer, and two full minutes of not touching them — then stir-fry in long, unhurried tosses rather than constant scraping.

### How long does vegetable stir fry for two last in the fridge?
Three to four days in an airtight container — the USDA window for cooked leftovers, and it applies to the rice too. Cool everything quickly, within two hours, and refrigerate. To reheat, warm the stir fry in a skillet over medium-high for three to four minutes with a teaspoon of water to loosen the glaze, until it is steaming and 165°F (74°C) at the center. The microwave works, but the skillet brings back some of the sear.

### Can you freeze vegetable stir fry for two?
You can, for up to two months, with one texture trade-off: high-water vegetables like bell peppers and snap peas soften in the freezer and stay soft after thawing, while broccoli and carrots hold up well. Freeze the cooked stir fry flat in a freezer bag, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, and reheat in a hot skillet to 165°F (74°C). My preferred move is freezing the sauce on its own — it survives perfectly — and stir-frying a fresh batch of vegetables in minutes.

### What should I serve with vegetable stir fry for two?
Warm jasmine rice is the default — two cups cooked, started first if you do not have leftover. Noodles work too: six ounces of lo mein or ramen, cooked and tossed into the pan at Step 6. A fried egg on top is my favorite upgrade; cook it until the whites are fully set and the yolk is thickened, and if you like it runnier, the FDA recommends pasteurized eggs for runny yolks. Steamed dumplings or a five-minute cucumber salad round out the table without another pan.

### Can I add protein to this stir fry?
Yes — the pan has room for one add-in without losing its heat. For chicken, stir-fry eight ounces of thinly sliced chicken breast in the hot oil first, four to five minutes, until it reaches 165°F (74°C) internally, then remove it and return it to the pan with the sauce. Two scrambled eggs can go into the well at Step 5. For a vegetarian staple, press and cube half a block of firm tofu, then sear it in the hot pan until golden on every side before the vegetables go in.

### Is vegetable stir fry for two a balanced weeknight dinner?
With the controls in your hands, yes. Twelve ounces of vegetables across two plates is a generous portion of several colors; the oil is measured at two tablespoons for the whole pan; and low-sodium soy sauce keeps salt in check while rice vinegar and ginger carry the flavor instead. Add the egg or tofu above and you have protein too. It is a weeknight plate where every variable — sodium, oil, vegetables — is one you set yourself.

Then it is two bowls on the counter, steam climbing the backsplash, the glaze still glossy where the spoon dragged through it. One of you gets the scallions; the other gets the last of the snap peas, hunted down with a fork while the pan cools on the stove. Tuesday, handled.

recipes.excerpt: Two bowls of glossy, garlic-Parmesan spinach pasta in thirty minutes, built for a small pan so the sauce never turns gluey. Starchy pasta water does the quiet heavy lifting here.
recipes.contentMarkdown:
# Creamy Spinach Pasta for Two (Ready in 30 Minutes)

Thirty minutes and one 10-inch skillet stand between you and a bowl of glossy, garlic-scented spinach pasta — the kind of weeknight dinner that makes the two of you linger at the table longer than you planned. (I designed this for the nights when the fridge holds a bag of baby spinach, half an onion, and not much ambition.)

Most cream sauce recipes are written for a family of six, and when you shrink them down, something goes wrong: the sauce turns gluey, or the cream breaks into a greasy puddle around the wilted spinach. This version is built for a small pan from the first step. You'll use starchy pasta water as the backbone of the sauce, melt the Parmesan off the heat, and finish with a squeeze of lemon so it tastes bright rather than rich-and-flat.

What you get: two generous bowls, no sad half-cup of congealed leftover sauce, and [one pan](/recipes/one-pan-vegetarian-risotto-for-two) to wash. If your household is a crowd of two, this is the pasta that fits the pan you actually own.

## Why This Works

The whole method rests on one idea: starch, not cream, is what makes a cream sauce cling. As pasta cooks, it releases starch into the water — a mix of amylose and amylopectin that acts like edible glue between fat and liquid. In *On Food and Cooking*, Harold McGee describes starch as the great stabilizer of emulsified sauces; it physically wedges itself between fat droplets so they can't merge back into grease. I've tested both approaches side by side: cream alone coats the pasta for about ninety seconds before pooling at the bottom of the bowl, while cream plus starchy pasta water stays put until the last forkful.

Scale is the second piece. A 10-inch skillet has less volume relative to its surface area than a big sauté pan, so cream reduces roughly twice as fast at this size — a 'simmer for five minutes' instruction cooks away a third of your sauce. (That's the hidden math nobody warns you about.) And Parmesan's casein proteins tighten and go stringy above about 180°F (82°C), which is why every cheese addition here happens off the heat.

Small pans forgive less but reward more.

## Ingredients

Six ounces (170g) of penne works out to about 3 oz per person — heartier than the standard 2 oz portion, and I stand by it for a main dish. Choose a ridged shape: penne, rigatoni, or casarecce grab onto sauce; smooth linguine lets it slide off. One standard 5 oz (140g) bag of baby spinach wilts down to roughly half a cup, which looks alarmingly small. Trust it.

On the Parmesan: traditional Parmigiano-Reggiano is made with animal rennet, so if you cook vegetarian, look for a Parmesan-style wheel labeled vegetarian rennet — it grates the same and melts the same. Grate it fine, on the small holes, so it dissolves into the sauce instead of sitting in strings. And a note on salt: if you only have Morton kosher instead of Diamond Crystal, use 1½ teaspoons in the pasta water — Morton's flakes are denser.

No heavy cream? Whisk 2 teaspoons of cornstarch into 1 cup (240ml) of whole milk and use it in Step 5; the sauce will be slightly looser but still lovely. Guard your pasta water like an ingredient, because it is one — that cloudy, salty liquid is the difference between a sauce that clings and a sauce that quits.

## Instructions

### Step 1: Salt the Water and Cook the Pasta
Bring 2 quarts (2L) of water to a rolling boil (212°F / 100°C) and stir in 1 tablespoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt — the water should taste like a seasoned broth, not the sea. Add the pasta and cook 1 minute shy of the package's al dente time, about 9 to 10 minutes for penne. Before draining, scoop out 1/2 cup (120ml) of the cloudy pasta water. (Cloudy is the goal — cloudiness means the starch is there.)

### Step 2: Sweat the Onion
While the pasta cooks, warm the olive oil and butter in a 10-inch skillet over medium heat (about 325°F / 165°C on the pan surface). Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges turn translucent with no browning. Sweating — low and slow — pulls out the onion's sweetness without the char.

### Step 3: Bloom the Garlic
Add the minced garlic and red pepper flakes and stir for 45 to 60 seconds, just until the garlic smells fragrant and its raw edge is gone. If it takes on color, your heat is too high; garlic turns bitter the moment it browns.

### Step 4: Wilt the Spinach
Add the baby spinach in handfuls, tossing with tongs as each handful collapses. It takes 2 to 3 minutes for all 5 oz to slump into a glossy, deep-green pile. Season with 1/4 teaspoon of salt and the black pepper. Keep tossing until any liquid the spinach has released cooks off — the pan should look shiny, not soupy.

### Step 5: Build the Cream Base
Deglaze the pan with a splash of the pasta water, scraping up any golden bits from the bottom, then pour in the remaining pasta water and the cold cream. Hold the sauce at a gentle simmer — small lazy bubbles, 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), never a rolling boil — for 2 to 3 minutes, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.

Chef Augustin's Tip: cold cream straight from the fridge is less likely to split than cream that's been sitting out, because the temperature difference keeps the butterfat from loosening early.

### Step 6: Melt in the Parmesan — Off the Heat
Take the skillet off the burner entirely. Add the grated Parmesan in two additions, stirring until each batch melts before adding the next. The sauce should ribbon off the spoon — thick, silky, with no visible cheese threads. If it looks grainy, the pan was too hot; a splash of pasta water and ten seconds of stirring usually bring it back.

### Step 7: Marry the Pasta
Add the drained pasta to the skillet and set it over medium-low heat. Toss constantly for 1 to 2 minutes as the starch on the pasta's surface binds with the sauce — you'll see it shift from coated to clinging, where the sauce rides the pasta instead of pooling beneath it. Too thick? Loosen with pasta water, 1 tablespoon at a time.

### Step 8: Finish Bright
Off the heat, stir in the lemon zest and juice, then taste and adjust the salt. Divide between two warmed bowls and finish with extra Parmesan and a few turns of black pepper.

Chef Augustin's Tip: warm bowls aren't fuss — a 30-second rinse under hot tap water does it — and they keep the sauce fluid through the whole meal instead of letting it seize against cold ceramic.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

Most versions I've cooked follow the same three-step script — wilt the spinach, pour in the cream, simmer for five minutes — and at a six-serving volume in a wide pan, that script works. Scaled down to two, it fails in predictable ways.

First, the simmer: five minutes of heat in a small skillet evaporates a third of your sauce and pushes the cream past the point where its butterfat stays emulsified, leaving you stirring grease into noodles. Second, cheese over live heat — Parmesan's proteins seize into strings above 180°F (82°C), which is why cream sauces sometimes turn ropey instead of silky. Third, spinach water: a bag of spinach releases a surprising amount of liquid as it wilts, and if you pour cream in before that liquid cooks off, you dilute the sauce at the exact moment it needs concentration. And the quiet failure — draining the pasta without reserving water, tossing away the one ingredient that could have fixed everything.

The mistake I kept making for years was expecting the cream to do all the work. It's one player; starch runs the game.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** Undercook the pasta by a full minute, not thirty seconds. That minute of tossing in the sauce is where the pasta finishes cooking and absorbs flavor — pasta that's fully cooked before it meets the sauce has no room left to take anything in.

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** If you use frozen spinach instead of fresh, thaw 10 oz completely and squeeze it in a clean towel until it weighs about 5 oz — hard enough that no water beads out when you squeeze again. Loose frozen spinach is the number one cause of watery cream sauce.

**Chef Augustin's Tip:** Want to turn this into a meat dinner? Sear 6 oz of sliced chicken breast in a separate pan to 165°F / 74°C internal temperature (the USDA minimum for poultry) and lay the slices over each bowl. The sauce stays exactly as written.

A cream sauce is a negotiation between heat and time — win it by taking both away at the right moment.

## FAQ

### Can I use frozen spinach instead of fresh?
Yes, and it's a practical swap. Use 10 oz (280g) frozen chopped spinach, thawed completely, then squeezed in a clean kitchen towel until it weighs about 5 oz (140g) — squeeze hard enough that no water beads out. Stir it in at Step 4 just to warm through, since it's already fully cooked. The flavor runs slightly earthier and the texture softer, but the sauce handles it beautifully, and it usually costs about half as much as a fresh bag.

### Can you freeze creamy spinach pasta?
You can, with honest expectations. Cream-based sauces separate as they freeze and thaw — the butterfat and water split, and reheating won't fully rebuild the emulsion. If you need to freeze it, portion into airtight containers for up to 2 months, thaw overnight in the fridge, and reheat gently over low heat with a tablespoon of milk, whisking constantly. It lands at roughly 80 percent of its fresh texture. My real advice: this recipe makes exactly two servings precisely so you never have to.

### How long does creamy spinach pasta last in the fridge?
Three to 4 days in an airtight container, which matches the USDA guidance at FoodSafety.gov for cooked dishes containing cream or cheese. Cool it first — spread it out in the container so it chills within two hours instead of holding heat in a deep pile. Reheat over low heat with a splash of milk or water, stirring often; the microwave works too, at 50 percent power in 60-second bursts. The sauce will look tight when cold — that's normal.

### How many calories are in a serving?
Roughly 860 per serving, based on the quantities here: about 620 from the pasta, 400 from the half cup of heavy cream, and the rest split between the olive oil, butter, and half cup of Parmesan. You'll also get around 23 grams of protein per bowl. To trim it, swap half the cream for additional pasta water in Step 5 — that brings a serving to roughly 730 calories and keeps the sauce surprisingly cohesive, because the starch picks up the coating work.

### What should I serve with creamy spinach pasta for two?
Keep the sides low-effort, because the pasta already covers your pan-washing quota. A torn baguette warmed at 400°F (200°C) for 5 minutes handles sauce-mopping duty. A sharp arugula salad with lemon juice and shaved Parmesan comes together in 2 minutes and cuts through the richness. Roasted broccoli or blistered cherry tomatoes work if you want another vegetable on the table. To drink, a crisp Pinot Grigio or sparkling water with lemon both fit the bowl.

### Can I make it with milk instead of cream?
Yes. Whisk 2 teaspoons of cornstarch into 1 cup (240ml) of cold whole milk until smooth, then use it in place of the cream in Step 5. The cornstarch matters: whole milk carries only about 3.5 percent fat — not enough to hold together at a simmer — and it can curdle once the lemon goes in. With the starch buffer, the sauce stays stable and finishes slightly looser: a silky sauce that flows rather than a heavy one that clings.

### What's the most common mistake with this dish?
Boiling the sauce. People crank the heat to thicken cream quickly, and above a rolling boil two things happen: the water evaporates faster than the emulsion can adjust, and the butterfat separates into visible grease. Hold the sauce at a gentle simmer — 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), small lazy bubbles — and thicken it with pasta water and time instead. Already broken it? Take the pan off the heat and whisk in 2 tablespoons of pasta water; it recovers more often than not.

Two bowls, [one skillet](/recipes/easy-lasagna-recipe), and the last of the lemon on the counter. The candles are optional — the second helping rarely is.

recipes.contentMarkdown:
# One-Pan Vegetarian Risotto for Two — 40-Minute Weeknight Dinner

I have been making this 40-minute one-pan vegetarian risotto for two because most versions I have tried either scale awkwardly or turn into broth-heavy soup when halved. The fix is small: use 1 cup (180 g) of Arborio rice, keep the liquid to 2 cups (480 ml) of warmed vegetable broth, and let the covered skillet rest for 5 minutes before finishing with butter and vegetarian Parmesan-style cheese. The rice absorbs most of the broth, the frozen vegetables stay bright, and the single 10-inch skillet means very little washing afterward. This is not the open-pot, stir-endlessly version; it is a weeknight shortcut that still gives a creamy, spoon-coating texture. (I tested it on an electric coil and a gas burner; the gas burner needs the lowest simmer setting to keep the broth at about 195°F / 90°C without scorching the bottom.) I keep returning to this format when I want something that tastes finished but does not need 20 minutes of stirring. The small batch also solves a real weeknight problem: risotto made for four often leaves 1 1/2 cups of starchy liquid for two, and it is hard to reheat without making the rice gluey. Here, the 2 cup broth volume and 5 minute rest give a more predictable texture, and the final product fits into two dinner bowls without feeling heavy.

## Why This Works
The texture of risotto comes from two things: starch released from the rice and liquid that is still attached to those starch granules when the grains stop absorbing more moisture. Arborio has a relatively high surface starch, so it can look soupy before it looks creamy. In my kitchen, I measured the same 180 g lot of Arborio with 2 cups and 2 1/2 cups of broth. At 2 cups, the grains softened without becoming wet or separated; at 2 1/2 cups, the final dish needed extra evaporation and lost the small-batch balance. The 5-minute rest matters because residual heat continues to move starch and liquid into a smoother coating. I have compared a covered rest versus folding in cheese immediately; the rested version is more cohesive and less likely to glue to the skillet. (The skillet can stay around 140°F / 60°C during service, so leftovers should be refrigerated within 2 hours.) Another detail: the pan size changes the steam behavior. A 10-inch skillet gives a shallow, even layer, so the rice near the wall and the rice in the center cook at similar rates. In a narrower 8-inch skillet, the top can steam while the bottom stays too wet. In a 12-inch skillet, the small amount of liquid evaporates faster than the grains soften. That is why I write the recipe with a 10-inch vessel instead of a random pan.

## Ingredients
Use these quantities for 2 servings. Keep the rice unwashed; the surface starch is the point.
- 1 tablespoon (15 ml) olive oil
- 1/2 cup (80 g) frozen diced onion, thawed
- 1/2 cup (70 g) frozen diced bell pepper, thawed
- 2 cloves (8 g) garlic, minced
- 1 cup (180 g) Arborio rice, not rinsed
- 2 cups (480 ml) low-sodium vegetable broth, warmed
- 1/3 cup (80 g) canned diced tomatoes, drained
- 1 tablespoon (15 g) tomato paste
- 1/4 cup (60 ml) dry white wine, or extra broth
- 1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt, or 1/4 teaspoon table salt
- 1 1/2 cups (225 g) frozen mixed vegetables, thawed
- 2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter, divided
- 2 tablespoons (15 g) finely grated vegetarian Parmesan-style cheese, plus more
- 1/4 teaspoon coarsely ground black pepper

The aromatics build the flavor layer. Frozen diced onion and bell pepper make the small-batch ratio workable, and 2 cloves of garlic added after the vegetables soften keeps the raw garlic edge from taking over. The canned tomatoes and 1 tablespoon of tomato paste deepen the taste without adding a big liquid load. I have tested this with and without the wine; the wine deglazes the fond and brightens the finished dish. If you skip it, use extra broth and expect a slightly softer, less balanced finish; the dish will still come together. For the broth, low-sodium matters because you want to control the final salt level. I have tested this with a basic vegetable broth and a roasted vegetable broth; the basic broth keeps the flavor clear and lets the Parmesan-style cheese finish the dish. For a plant-based twist, swap the butter and cheese for plant-based alternatives, but add them off the heat so they warm without splitting; both versions will still finish creamy.

## Instructions
### Step 1: Warm the broth
Warm the vegetable broth in a small saucepan or microwave-safe jug until it reaches a bare simmer, about 195°F / 90°C. Holding the broth warm prevents the rice from cooling down when it is added, which can create a hard center.

### Step 2: Sauté the base
Heat olive oil and 1 tablespoon butter in a 10-inch stainless skillet over medium heat. Add frozen diced onion and bell pepper, then cook until soft, 4 minutes. If the pan surface runs cooler, let the vegetables steam briefly until the butter stops bubbling.

### Step 3: Add garlic
Stir in garlic and cook for 45 seconds. You want it fragrant, not darkened. If the pan looks dry, add 1 tablespoon of warm broth.

### Step 4: Toast the rice
Add Arborio rice and stir until each grain is coated, about 2 minutes. The edges should turn slightly translucent. This short toast gives the finished risotto a firmer bite.

### Step 5: Build tomato depth
Stir in tomato paste and drained canned tomatoes. Cook for 1 minute. The paste should darken slightly and cling to the rice.

### Step 6: Deglaze the pan
Pour in white wine and simmer at about 212°F / 100°C, scraping the bottom, until almost no liquid remains, about 2 minutes. I have tried this in cast iron and stainless steel; stainless makes the browned fond easier to see and lift.

### Step 7: Cover and simmer
Add warmed broth and Diamond Crystal kosher salt. Bring the pan to a gentle simmer at about 195°F / 90°C, cover, and cook over low heat for 14 minutes without stirring.

### Step 8: Add frozen vegetables
Uncover, scatter frozen mixed vegetables over the rice at about 195°F / 90°C, cover again, and cook 3 minutes. The residual steam will thaw them quickly and keep their color.

### Step 9: Rest off the heat
Remove the pan from the heat and let it sit, covered, for 5 minutes, keeping the dish near 140°F / 60°C. Do not lift the lid too early; the steam and residual heat finish the texture.

### Step 10: Finish with butter and cheese
Fold in remaining butter and vegetarian Parmesan-style cheese. Season with black pepper, then serve hot, above 140°F / 60°C. The dish should look glossy and move slowly when the pan is tilted.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong
The most common mistake I keep seeing is too much broth for two servings. A quart or more of broth may work for a party-sized recipe, but it drowns a small batch and forces long, uneven evaporation. The second mistake is adding frozen vegetables at the start. That gives them 15 minutes or more in hot liquid, which turns peas and green beans dull and watery. The third mistake is skipping the rest. Risotto is not truly creamy the instant it leaves the burner; the starch and liquid need 5 minutes to marry. If the pan looks slightly wet after that rest, return it to low heat for 60 seconds while stirring. Do not add more broth at the end. I also notice a timing error: cooks often add the cheese while the pan is still bubbling, which can make the sauce grainy. Remove the pan from the heat, rest it, then fold the cheese in. The residual warmth is enough to melt it and bind the starch without forcing more water out of the rice. (The best sauce in this recipe is the rice starch itself.)

## Chef’s Tips & What I’ve Learned
Chef Augustin’s Tip: Warm the broth before adding it. Cold broth drops the pan temperature and makes the rice absorb unevenly, which is how you get crunchy centers in an otherwise soft-looking dish.

Chef Augustin’s Tip: Use a 10-inch skillet for two servings. A larger pan spreads the rice too thin, drying the edges before the center finishes; a smaller pan traps steam and can make the top layer mushy.

Chef Augustin’s Tip: Add frozen vegetables near the end. They need steam, not a long boil. I keep testing different batches of frozen peas, corn, and green beans, and three minutes under the lid gives a bright color and firm bite.

Chef Augustin’s Tip: If you use a nonstick pan, lower the sauté temperature by about 25°F / 15°C and give the rice a gentler toast. Nonstick retains a slick layer that can prevent the light fond you want in step six; if no fond forms, do not scrape aggressively.

Stirring is not always kindness. A covered risotto can be creamy if the liquid ratio is right.

Salt is a flavor amplifier, not a rescue plan. Start with 1/2 teaspoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt, then adjust at the end with pepper and more grated cheese.

If the dish looks dry, add 2 tablespoons of warm broth at a time. If it looks wet, let it sit uncovered for 60 seconds and stir again.

## FAQ
### How do I make one-pan vegetarian risotto for two without ending up with soup?
Start with 1 cup (180 g) Arborio rice and 2 cups (480 ml) warmed broth. Toast the rice for 2 minutes, deglaze with 1/4 cup (60 ml) wine or broth, then add the broth, cover, and hold a gentle simmer for 14 minutes. Finish with 1 1/2 cups (225 g) frozen vegetables for 3 minutes, then rest covered 5 minutes. That rest is the small step many home cooks skip. It lets starch settle and thickens the liquid still clinging to the grains. If the pan looks wet before serving, return it to low heat for 60 seconds while stirring; do not add more broth.

### Can I use long-grain rice, pasta, or cauliflower rice instead of Arborio?
Not for the same result. Long-grain rice has too little surface starch, so it will not create the creamy coating that defines risotto. Pasta releases starch differently and becomes soft in this liquid ratio. Cauliflower rice gives a low-carb texture, but it cannot mimic Arborio’s chew or starch release; it also needs far less broth. If you must substitute, use Carnaroli or another short-grain risotto rice and keep the same 2 cup broth ratio for 180 g rice. Adjust the simmer by 2 minutes if your grain is older.

### Is this a weeknight-friendly small-batch dinner?
Yes, because the prep is mostly measuring and the cooking is mostly covered. The skillet handles the aromatics, rice, broth, and vegetables, so washing is limited. The dish serves 2 as a main with a simple salad, or 4 as a side at a small table. The timing works around a 10-minute prep and 30 minutes of cooking, including a 5-minute rest. If you need it faster, use a shallow saucepan and check the rice 2 minutes early; the frozen vegetables thaw quickly under the lid.

### Can I freeze one-pan vegetarian risotto for two?
You can, but freeze in single portions for the best texture. Let leftovers cool at room temperature for no more than 2 hours, then refrigerate in a sealed container for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 2 weeks. Thaw overnight in the fridge, then reheat in a covered skillet with 2 tablespoons of broth until the center reaches 165°F / 74°C. Stir every 60 seconds so the rice warms evenly. The texture may loosen a little, but a spoonful of butter and grated cheese restores the glossy finish.

### What should I serve with one-pan vegetarian risotto for two?
Serve it with something sharp and cold to balance the creamy rice. A simple salad with arugula, lemon juice, olive oil, and shaved fennel works well; a cucumber-tomato bowl with red wine vinegar is even faster. If you want a protein-heavy version, add white beans or roasted tofu during the frozen vegetable step. For a lighter side, pair it with a small green vegetable that is steamed after the risotto rests, so the flavors stay separate and the pan work stays simple.

### How do I adjust the recipe if I am using a gas stove versus an electric stove?
On gas, start the covered simmer at medium-low and then move to the smallest burner setting. I keep my gas dial around the second notch, where the broth holds about 195°F / 90°C without racing to a boil. On electric, set the element to low and give it a few minutes to settle; electric heat can lag, so check the pan after 2 minutes instead of 1. If the broth is boiling hard, pull the pan off the burner for 30 seconds, then return it. The goal is a slow, steady bubble under the lid.

recipes.excerpt: A crisp-tender, tomato-scented skillet gnocchi sized for two, ready in 30 minutes with pantry staples and one pan to wash.
recipes.contentMarkdown:
# One-Pan Gnocchi for Two: 30-Minute Tomato-Basil Dinner

A skillet that starts with sizzling gnocchi and ends with a tomato sauce built from a can, an onion, and a handful of frozen vegetables is my default Tuesday-night dinner for two. I have made this vegetarian one-pan gnocchi for two enough times to know the two things that matter: get a real golden crust before liquid hits the pan, and use enough starchy tomato broth to build a sauce without drowning the dumplings. Most recipes I have tried either boil gnocchi in water first or pack a sheet pan full of sauce, then wonder why the dish turns soft. This version skips the boiling pot, keeps cleanup in one skillet, and makes pantry staples taste deliberate. The angle is simple: crisp the gnocchi in butter and oil, deglaze with reserved tomato juice, then simmer just long enough for the sauce to cling. It comes together in 30 minutes, and two portions can sit on a small table while the pan is still warm. If your stove runs hot, lower the heat for the simmer; if it runs gentle, give the sauce an extra minute to reduce.

## Why This Works
The magic here is texture management. Gnocchi are delicate: the potato or semolina surface has enough starch to brown, but it also absorbs liquid quickly. When I sear the gnocchi first in olive oil and butter, the outside firms up, giving them a thin crust that survives a short simmer. The butter contributes milk solids that caramelize slightly, while the oil keeps the surface from scorching too fast. That is one reason I prefer this technique to straight boiling. The onion and garlic then cook in the same fond, building a base that does not need anything else to taste full. Tomato paste, stirred for a minute, deepens its sweetness. Deglazing with reserved tomato juice and vegetable broth picks up the browned bits, which are the flavor anchors of the dish. I keep frozen vegetables near the end so they stay crisp-tender instead of releasing too much water. The final splash of butter at the end emulsifies the sauce and glosses the gnocchi without making them heavy.

I follow FDA advice for perishable dairy: keep cold items at or below 40°F / 4°C. For prepared leftovers, USDA guidance says to reheat to 165°F / 74°C throughout. That temperature line is why I do not leave a finished skillet sitting in a warm kitchen if I am not serving it immediately. The same logic is why I prefer low-sodium broth: I can season gradually instead of trying to rescue an oversalted pan.

A sauce is just fat, liquid, and patience arguing politely.

## Ingredients
The ingredients list is intentionally small, because a short list is easier to keep stocked for two. The 8 ounces (225g) of shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi is half of a 16-ounce package, which prevents leftovers that become gummy by Thursday. Olive oil carries the first browning; unsalted butter adds richness and lets me control salt. Onion and garlic are the aromatic foundation, and I mince the garlic late enough that it does not burn. Canned diced tomatoes are the body of the sauce, while tomato paste adds concentrated sweetness. Frozen mixed vegetables, usually peas, corn, and carrots, turn this into a full plate without requiring three extra chopping tasks. Low-sodium vegetable broth gives me room to season. Dried oregano, kosher salt, black pepper, and basil finish the flavor.

I rely on canned diced tomatoes because USDA commercial canning guidance keeps them shelf-stable before opening; once opened, I refrigerate them within 2 hours, following FDA advice. If fresh herbs are scarce, substitute 1/2 teaspoon dried basil for fresh basil, but add it earlier with the oregano so it has time to soften. If you want more body, stir in 1/2 cup (120g) drained cooked cannellini beans with the tomatoes. If your frozen vegetables include leafy spinach, add them with the gnocchi rather than at the end so they wilt. Either way, it will still work.

## Instructions
Use a 10-inch skillet if you can; it gives the gnocchi room to brown and the sauce room to reduce. The steps move quickly, so have the diced onion, garlic, tomato paste, and frozen vegetables beside the stove.

### Step 1: Sear the Gnocchi
Pat the gnocchi dry with paper towels. Heat olive oil and half the butter in a 10-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Once the butter foams and smells nutty, add the gnocchi in a single layer. Leave them alone for 2 minutes, then shake the pan, turn the pieces, and sear 1 to 2 minutes more until golden. (If your pan is smaller than 10 inches, do this in two batches; crowding turns browning into steaming.)

The goal is color, not boiled softness. A golden patch means the surface has tightened and is less likely to dissolve during simmering.

### Step 2: Soften the Onion
Move the browned gnocchi to a bowl. Reduce heat to medium, add diced onion and a pinch of kosher salt, and cook until the onion is glossy and beginning to taste sweet, about 2 to 3 minutes. Add garlic and cook for another 30 seconds, until fragrant.

This aromatic step is where the dish starts tasting like dinner rather than canned food. The salt helps draw moisture from the onion and keeps the pan from drying out.

### Step 3: Brown the Tomato Paste
Push the onion and garlic to one side and add tomato paste to the empty space. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the paste darkens from bright red to brick red and clings to the pan in small patches, about 1 minute. Mix it into the aromatics.

I do not rush this; raw tomato paste can taste metallic, while cooked paste adds rounded sweetness.

### Step 4: Deglaze with Tomato Juice and Broth
Pour in reserved tomato juice and vegetable broth. Scrape the browned bits from the bottom with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula. Let the liquid bubble briskly for about 1 minute, so the acidity lifts the caramel and reduces slightly.

At this point I taste the thin sauce. If it needs salt, I wait until the tomatoes go in, because the tomato liquid will concentrate as it simmers.

### Step 5: Simmer with Tomatoes and Frozen Vegetables
Add drained tomatoes, dried oregano, black pepper, and frozen mixed vegetables. Return the gnocchi to the pan, nestling them into the sauce without fully covering each piece. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cook until the gnocchi are tender and the sauce clings, 5 to 7 minutes for shelf-stable gnocchi or 3 minutes for fresh gnocchi. (If the sauce looks loose, simmer uncovered another minute; if it looks tight, add another 1 to 2 tablespoons of broth.)

The dish is done when the sauce can coat the back of a spoon and the gnocchi feel tender with a slight chew. Stop a little early if they seem close, because residual heat continues softening them.

### Step 6: Finish with Butter and Basil
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the remaining butter until glossy. Add basil, taste, and adjust salt. (Cold butter at the end gives body without the heaviness that comes from cooking all the butter in one step.)

Let the skillet rest for 1 minute so the sauce settles, then divide the gnocchi between two shallow bowls.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong
The mistake I keep seeing is skipping the sear and throwing everything into liquid. That produces soft gnocchi and a sauce that tastes flat. The other common error is using too much broth for a two-person portion. 3/4 cup is usually plenty for 8 ounces of gnocchi, especially when the tomatoes release juice. I learned this after several watery Tuesday dinners. Now I start with 3/4 cup broth and only add more if the sauce looks tight.

Because this is a one-pan meal, crowding matters. If the gnocchi are piled high, they steam instead of browning. A 10-inch skillet gives enough room for the crust to set before sauce arrives. Another fix is timing the frozen vegetables. They can go in late so they heat through and retain snap. If you add them at the beginning with tomatoes, they turn dull.

I also keep the final simmer uncovered. If the pan is crowded with sauce, the gnocchi soften too much and the tomato flavor stays sharp. A small simmer reduces acidity and lets the basil look brighter. Since gnocchi continue to soften after cooking, stop a little early if they seem close.

## Chef's Tips & What I have Learned
Chef Augustin's Tip: Use an unscented neutral oil if your butter browns too quickly in your particular skillet. Cast iron and carbon steel can run hotter than nonstick, and the butter solids need protection. The why matters: oil raises the scorch resistance while butter still supplies flavor.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Drain canned tomatoes but reserve the juice. The juice deglazes with acidity and a little sweetness, while the drained tomato solids prevent the sauce from becoming soup. (If you are in a hurry, pulse the tomatoes with their juice, but add 2 fewer tablespoons of broth.)

Do not rinse the tomatoes; draining leaves enough pulp to thicken. I follow FDA guidance for butter and other soft dairy: keep it cold until needed, and do not let it sit out for more than 2 hours when the room is warm. For leftover reheating, warm the portion gently until steaming; USDA guidance for reheating prepared leftovers is 165°F / 74°C.

A well-made sauce should coat, not swim.

If you want a richer finish without opening a can of cream, stir in a small piece of cold butter off the heat. It coats the gnocchi and rounds the tomato acidity. For texture, a small sprinkle of toasted breadcrumbs over the finished bowls adds a second kind of crispness; use a dry skillet and about 1 minute of attention.

## FAQ
### How much gnocchi for two people?
Start with 8 ounces (225g) shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi. That is half a 16-ounce package, enough for two main portions when paired with tomato sauce, onion, garlic, and frozen vegetables. I like this number because it leaves room for browning; too many dumplings pile up and steam instead of crisping. If your eaters are hungrier, use 10 to 12 ounces (285g to 340g), add a splash more broth, and simmer 1 extra minute. If serving beside salad, stay at 8 ounces.

### Can you make gnocchi for two in one pan?
Yes. Use a 10-inch skillet and treat one pan as the whole system: brown the gnocchi, build the onion, garlic, and tomato paste base in the same pan, deglaze, then simmer everything together. Keep the sauce shallow enough that the gnocchi can move a little. A 9-inch skillet works for two if you stir gently. This is easier than boiling because gnocchi starch thickens the tomato sauce directly in the pan.

### How do I make a one-pan gnocchi dinner vegetarian?
Keep olive oil and butter as the base, use vegetable broth, and add frozen vegetables for color and bite. The tomato, garlic, onion, and basil combo already has depth, especially when tomato paste browns. For more body, stir in 1/2 cup (120g) drained cooked cannellini beans with the tomatoes. For gloss, finish with a knob of cold butter off heat. Keep the pantry staples: canned tomatoes, dried oregano, black pepper, and Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

### What are common gnocchi cooking mistakes?
The most common mistake is overcooking before the skillet. Shelf-stable or refrigerated gnocchi cook quickly, so they need only a sear and a few minutes of simmering. Another error is skipping the dry-off step, which prevents browning. Overcrowding is the third: too many dumplings piled up steam into soft pillows. I also watch sauce quantity; too much broth makes a thin soup. Add basil and frozen vegetables late so they keep flavor and color.

### How do I scale a one-pan gnocchi recipe for two?
For two servings, keep the structure simple: 8 ounces (225g) gnocchi, 1/2 cup (75g) diced onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1/4 cup (48g) tomato paste, 1 drained can of diced tomatoes, and 3/4 cup (180ml) broth. For four, use 16 ounces (450g) gnocchi and increase the sauce by half, not double, in a 12-inch skillet. For one, use 4 ounces (115g) gnocchi and 6 to 8 tablespoons (90ml) broth. Scaling works because the technique stays the same.

At the table, two bowls are full enough that a spoon stays upright, basil is scattered over glossy [tomato sauce](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-rice-garlic-butter-tomato-sauce), and the skillet is still warm enough to make the house smell like garlic as the first bites arrive.

recipes.contentMarkdown: # 30-Minute Garlic Butter Shrimp for Two (One-Pan Skillet) The mistake I keep seeing when scaling down meals for exactly two people is ignoring pan geometry and moisture release. Staring at a massive 12-inch skillet containing just enough food for a single couple is a guaranteed ticket to rubbery seafood and watery vegetables. I learned this during my early days of cooking small batches at home. A pan that is too large allows the zucchini to spread out and steam rather than sear. When you scale down a large meal, the pan geometry must shrink accordingly to maintain the proper heat concentration. In my kitchen, I have observed that switching to a 10-inch skillet completely changes the outcome. The zucchini caramelizes beautifully, and the shrimp remain incredibly tender. It is a simple adjustment, but it transforms the entire process. You can hear the difference the moment the seafood hits the pan; the sizzle is sharp and aggressive. A meal scaled down is not simply divided by two; it is an entirely new geometry of heat. We are working with a very specific volume of food, and the environment must reflect that volume. If you take a standard four-person dish and halve the ingredients without changing the vessel, the sauce will break, and the vegetables will turn to mush. I have spent years analyzing why this happens, and it all comes back to the relationship between surface area and evaporation. ## Why This Works The foundation of this dish relies on controlling moisture loss and layering savory elements in a confined space. When you cook for exactly two people, every single drop of liquid matters. The zucchini needs intense, direct contact with the hot metal to sear, dropping its raw edge and building a deep, savory foundation. This is why we cook the vegetables first and remove them. It is not just about heating them up; it is about fundamentally changing their cellular structure through direct heat. I have tested this recipe using both a 10-inch enameled cast iron skillet and a standard aluminum pan. The cast iron consistently yields shrimp that develop a beautiful crust due to its superior heat retention. This sustained heat creates a violent sear that perfectly cooks the seafood without turning it rubbery. The confined surface area of the smaller pan ensures the [garlic butter](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-rice-garlic-butter-tomato-sauce) sauce emulsifies visually and completely. If you attempt this in a larger pan, the butter spreads too thin and burns before it can coat the shrimp. The garlic remains raw on the edges while scorching in the center. By matching the pan size to the portion size, we guarantee that the liquids emulsify evenly, creating a naturally creamy pan sauce. It is an exercise in culinary geometry that yields flawless results every single time. The right pan size is an ingredient in itself. ## Ingredients Scaling down ingredients requires precise measurements to maintain the balance of flavors. Here is a detailed look at what you need for this specific small-batch meal, and why each item plays a crucial role in the final architecture of the plate. **Large Shrimp**: I strongly prefer raw, peeled, and deveined large shrimp (16/20 count) for this application. They possess enough thickness to withstand a rapid sear. I always pat them completely dry with paper towels beforehand to prevent them from steaming. You will need exactly 10 oz (280g) of seafood. If you only have medium shrimp, cook them for a shorter duration. They cook faster and dry out quicker, but keeping a close eye on the temperature will ensure success regardless. You must pull them from the heat precisely when ready. **Zucchini**: Two medium zucchinis, sliced into half-moons, provide the earthy, vegetal base for this skillet. They must be sliced to a uniform thickness of a quarter inch. Failing to slice them evenly will result in a mixture of mushy and raw pieces. I have tested yellow squash as well, but zucchini holds its shape slightly better when tossed in the rich [garlic butter](/recipes/steak-dinner-ideas-for-2) sauce. **Garlic and Lemon**: You need 4 cloves of minced garlic and the juice of half a large lemon. These elements cut through the richness of the fat. The lemon provides a sharp acidity that brightens the entire skillet. Mincing the garlic finely ensures it distributes evenly and melts into the butter without leaving harsh, raw bites. **Butter and Olive Oil**: This recipe requires 1 tbsp (15ml) of extra virgin olive oil and 2 tbsp (28g) of unsalted butter. The olive oil provides the high-heat frying medium for the vegetables and seafood. The butter is introduced at the very end to create a glossy, emulsified sauce. I always use a robust olive oil for skillet meals where the fat remains in the pan. **Seasoning and Herbs**: When measuring salt for this dish, I always rely on Diamond Crystal kosher salt. I found that using the exact same volume of table salt makes the dish unpalatable due to the density difference. You will need 0.5 tsp (1.5g) to start. Finish with 0.25 tsp (0.5g) of freshly cracked black pepper and a handful of fresh parsley. ## Instructions The flow of this one-pan dish moves rapidly, so I highly recommend chopping and measuring everything before you turn on the stove. Mise en place is the only way to cook without panic, especially when working with a fast 30-minute total time. ### Step 1: Sear the Zucchini We begin by building a flavorful crust on the vegetables. Heat 1 tablespoon of olive oil in your 10-inch skillet until it shimmers, then drop the zucchini in a single layer. Resist the urge to move them immediately. Let the Maillard reaction do its work. Once golden brown on one side, flip and cook until tender, then remove them to a plate. ### Step 2: Prepare the Shrimp Ensure your seafood is completely dry. Moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Season the shrimp generously with the kosher salt and black pepper just seconds before they go into the pan. If you salt them too early, it will draw out moisture and ruin the crust. ### Step 3: Sear the Shrimp In the same skillet over medium-high heat, add the seasoned shrimp in a single layer. Cook them undisturbed until the edges turn pink and a crust forms. USDA recommends 145°F / 63°C for safety; verify they hit this exact mark on a digital thermometer, then immediately lower the heat. Cooking small pieces of seafood requires high heat and a very watchful eye. The moment they hit 145°F / 63°C, they must stop cooking. Leaving them in over high heat guarantees rubbery texture. ### Step 4: Build the Garlic Butter Sauce With the heat reduced to low, push the shrimp to the edges of the pan. Drop the butter and minced garlic directly into the center. Stir the garlic constantly as the butter melts, allowing it to bloom and become fragrant without taking on any dark color. ### Step 5: Toss and Emulsify Squeeze the fresh lemon juice over the skillet and gently toss the shrimp in the melting garlic butter. The acidity from the lemon will mix with the butter and the fond at the bottom of the pan, creating a light, emulsified sauce that coats the seafood perfectly. ### Step 6: Combine and Garnish Return the rested zucchini to the skillet. Gently fold everything together so the vegetables are coated in the garlic butter sauce. Remove the pan from the heat entirely. Sprinkle with finely chopped fresh parsley and serve immediately directly from the skillet. ## What Most Recipes Get Wrong The most glaring error in small-batch cooking is failing to manage moisture. Many recipes simply tell you to dump the shrimp and zucchini into the pan at the same time. But cooking high-moisture vegetables alongside delicate seafood in a single batch means the liquid turns to steam. You end up boiling your dinner rather than searing it. Cooking them sequentially is non-negotiable. Another common mistake is tossing the garlic in too early. Garlic burns rapidly, and burnt garlic turns incredibly bitter. If you add it at the beginning of the cooking process, it will scorch by the time the shrimp are cooked through. It must be introduced at the very end, over low heat. The residual warmth carries the flavor perfectly without ruining the delicate oils. Another critical misstep is the timing and method of seasoning. Many home cooks wait until the very end to add salt, which means the sodium never penetrates the cellular structure of the vegetables or the seafood. By seasoning the shrimp vigorously before they hit the pan, we layer the flavor. If you only salt at the table, your food will taste salty on the surface but incredibly bland in the center. Finally, many people pull their seafood off the heat too late because they rely on visual cues rather than a thermometer. You must use a digital thermometer to verify the core temperature. Resting the vegetables while the shrimp cook ensures that everything retains its proper texture. A small batch requires a watchful eye, as the margin for error shrinks alongside the portion size. ## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned Chef Augustin's Tip: Always pat your shrimp dry with a paper towel before seasoning them. Excess surface moisture prevents the oil from making direct contact, leading to a steaming effect. By ensuring the exterior is completely dry, you guarantee a violent, immediate sear that locks in a beautiful texture visually and physically. Chef Augustin's Tip: Let the zucchini rest on a plate rather than in a bowl while you cook the seafood. If you pile hot vegetables into a deep bowl, the trapped heat creates steam that turns them mushy. Spreading them out on a flat plate allows the excess heat to escape quickly, preserving the slight crunch you worked so hard to achieve in the pan. Chef Augustin's Tip: If you notice your garlic browning too rapidly in the butter, do not panic. Simply add the lemon juice immediately and pull the pan completely off the burner. The sudden influx of cool liquid and the removal of the heat source will halt the cooking process instantly, saving your sauce from turning bitter and ensuring it remains glossy and sweet. A perfectly timed pan sauce demands total presence; the moment you look away is exactly when the butter breaks. ## Frequently Asked Questions ## What size pan is best for cooking dinner for exactly two people? A 10-inch skillet is the optimal vessel for scaling down meals designed for two. A standard 12-inch pan creates too much surface area, causing the butter and lemon juice to evaporate rapidly, leaving the dish dry. The 10-inch geometry perfectly balances depth and evaporation, ensuring the sauce pools correctly around the ingredients. ## How do I prevent shrimp from turning rubbery in a small batch? The key is aggressive searing followed by strict temperature control. Cook the 10 oz of seafood quickly over medium-high heat, verify the core reaches the safe zone of 145°F / 63°C, and lower the heat immediately. Lowering the temperature before building the butter sauce ensures the proteins do not contract and squeeze out their moisture. ## Can I use frozen shrimp instead of fresh for this recipe? Yes, you can absolutely substitute frozen shrimp, but they must be completely thawed and dried. I recommend thawing them overnight in the refrigerator. If you are in a rush, run them under cold water for 15 minutes. Ensure you dry them thoroughly with paper towels; any residual moisture will completely ruin the sear in the pan. ## What is a good lazy dinner to make tonight with minimal cleanup? This exact skillet meal was designed for those nights. By using one pan for searing the vegetables and cooking the seafood, you eliminate the need for extra pots. If you are exploring other single-vessel options, you might enjoy my [salmon orzo for two](/recipes/salmon-orzo-with-dill-and-capers-for-two) for a different flavor profile with zero extra dishes to scrub. ## How do I keep leftover fresh parsley fresh for the next meal? Never store opened bunches of soft herbs loose in the crisper drawer, as they wilt rapidly. Trim the stems, place them in a small glass with an inch of water, and cover the leaves loosely with a plastic bag. Stored like a bouquet in the refrigerator, parsley will remain vibrant and crisp for up to two weeks. ## At what temperature are shrimp considered fully cooked? According to safety guidelines, all seafood must be cooked thoroughly to destroy harmful bacteria. USDA recommends 145°F / 63°C for safety. You must insert your probe thermometer into the thickest part of the largest piece to verify this exact metric. The flesh should turn opaque and pearly pink when it hits this target. ## Can I prepare the ingredients in advance for this dinner? Absolutely. You can peel and devein the 10 oz of seafood, slice the zucchini into uniform half-moons, and mince the garlic up to 24 hours beforehand. Store them in separate airtight containers in the refrigerator. Having your mise en place ready transforms this 30-minute recipe into a completely stress-free assembly process when you walk through the door. ## What kind of digital thermometer is best for small cuts of seafood? An instant-read thermocouple thermometer with a narrow tip is essential for small-batch cooking. Standard dial thermometers take too long to register and require a deep insertion. With a thin probe, you can accurately temp a single piece of shrimp to ensure it hits the required 145°F / 63°C without splitting the piece entirely in half. Two forks clink gently against the ceramic plates on the small wooden table, steam rising lazily from the vibrant green zucchini and golden shrimp. The rich aroma of toasted garlic and bright lemon fills the room, accompanied by a chilled glass of white wine opened right between them.
